title: Conjugating small-field embeddings inside a large algebraically closed field
statement: Let $F$ and $K$ be fields [def-weil-field], with $K$ algebraically closed [def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $a,b:F\hookrightarrow K$ be field embeddings [def-pc-field-extension]. Let $P\subseteq K$ be the prime subfield, namely the smallest subfield containing $1$. Assume $$\max(\aleph_0,|F|)<\operatorname{trdeg}_{P}K,$$ where transcendence degree is as in [def-kun-transcendence-degree], $|F|$ is set cardinality, $\aleph_0=|\mathbf N|$, and all cardinalities are compared in a common universe. Then there is a field automorphism $\tau:K\xrightarrow{\sim}K$ (a bijective ring homomorphism) such that $\tau\circ a=b$.

source.place: Tag 04LR (lemma-groupoid-on-field-explain-points), proof, construction (3): extension of the isomorphism between i(k) and sigma(t(k)) by matching complementary transcendence bases and extending to algebraic closures.

proof.text: Put $\mu=\max(\aleph_0,|F|)$ and $\lambda=\operatorname{trdeg}_P K$. By [def-kun-transcendence-degree], $\lambda$ is a supremum of cardinalities of subsets of $K$. Every such cardinality is at most $|K|$, so $\lambda\leq|K|$. The hypothesis therefore gives $\mu<|K|$, and in particular both $|F|<|K|$ and $\aleph_0<|K|$.

source.place: Tag 04LR (lemma-groupoid-on-field-explain-points), proof, construction (3): make the large-transcendence-degree hypothesis quantitative.

proof.text: View $K$ first as an $F$-extension through $a$ and then as an $F$-extension through $b$; these are separate scalar structures on two copies of the same field [def-pc-field-extension]. Apply [lem-exc-transcendence-basis-exists] to obtain subsets $I,J\subseteq K$ with inclusion families $x:I\to K$ and $y:J\to K$ that are transcendence bases for these respective extension structures. Thus $x$ is independent over $a(F)$ and $K/a(F)(x)$ is algebraic, and the analogous assertions hold for $y,b(F)$ [def-weil-pbc-transcendence-basis].

source.place: Tag 04LR (lemma-groupoid-on-field-explain-points), proof, construction (3): choose bases directly over i(k) and sigma(t(k)), retaining those coefficient fields throughout.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-algclosed-transcendence-basis-cardinal-bound] to each of these two $F$-extension structures. It gives $|K|\leq\max(\mu,|I|)$ and $|K|\leq\max(\mu,|J|)$. Since $I,J$ are subsets of $K$, their cardinalities are at most $|K|$. If $|I|<|K|$, both entries of $\max(\mu,|I|)$ would be strictly smaller than $|K|$, contradicting the first inequality. Thus $|I|=|K|$; the same argument gives $|J|=|K|$. Consequently there is a bijection $e:I\xrightarrow{\sim}J$. This argument does not assume that $F$ is countable or that the cardinal $|K|$ is regular.

source.place: Tag 04LR (lemma-groupoid-on-field-explain-points), proof, construction (3): the two complementary bases have equal cardinality; elementary cardinal-order argument after the cited bound.

proof.text: Let $A=a(F)[x_i:i\in I]\subseteq K$ and $B=b(F)[y_j:j\in J]\subseteq K$ be the indicated polynomial subrings. Algebraic independence [def-weil-pbc-transcendence-basis] means that a polynomial expression in each basis has a unique formal polynomial over the abstract coefficient field $F$. Define $f:A\to B$ by replacing every coefficient $a(c)$ with $b(c)$, for $c\in F$, and every variable $x_i$ with $y_{e(i)}$. Addition and multiplication of polynomials show that this is a unital ring homomorphism. The reverse substitution replaces $b(c)$ with $a(c)$ and uses $e^{-1}$ on the variables. Both composites fix all coefficients and variables and hence all polynomials, so $f$ is a ring isomorphism, with $f(a(c))=b(c)$.

source.place: Tag 04LR (lemma-groupoid-on-field-explain-points), proof, construction (3): explicit coefficient and variable substitution; using the original coefficient fields avoids a separate preliminary extension between their relative algebraic closures.

proof.text: Inside the source and target copies of $K$, put $L=a(F)(x_i:i\in I)$ and $M=b(F)(y_j:j\in J)$, the smallest subfields containing $A$ and $B$. These consist exactly of fractions $u/v$ with $u,v\in A$, $v\ne0$, and respectively of fractions from $B$: the fractions form a subfield, and every subfield containing the subring contains these fractions. Define $h:L\to M$ by $h(u/v)=f(u)/f(v)$. The denominator stays nonzero because $f$ is injective. Equality of fractions is cross-multiplication, and $f$ preserves this equality, so $h$ is well-defined. The fraction formulas for addition and multiplication make $h$ a field homomorphism. Substitution with $f^{-1}$ gives its inverse. Therefore $h$ is a field isomorphism and $h(a(c))=b(c)$ for all $c\in F$.

source.place: Tag 04LR (lemma-groupoid-on-field-explain-points), proof, construction (3): the corresponding rational-function fields are isomorphic; fraction construction written explicitly.

proof.text: By [lem-exc-transcendence-basis-algebraic-closure], the source copy of $K$ is an algebraic closure of $L$ and the target copy is an algebraic closure of $M$. Give the target copy the $L$-extension map $L\xrightarrow{h}M\hookrightarrow K$. It is still algebraically closed. For any target element, take its nonzero polynomial relation over $M$ and apply $h^{-1}$ to every coefficient. At least one coefficient remains nonzero, and evaluation through this new $L$-extension map gives the original zero, so the target is algebraic over $L$. We now have two algebraic closures of the same field $L$, with specified structure maps. Clause (2) of [lem-pc-algebraic-closure-exists-unique] gives a field isomorphism $\tau:K\xrightarrow{\sim}K$ whose restriction to $L$ is $h$. Hence for every $c\in F$, $\tau(a(c))=h(a(c))=b(c)$, proving $\tau\circ a=b$. Bijectivity follows from this isomorphism conclusion, rather than from an arbitrary extension embedding.
